notes: Not the source: it forwards base::SysInfo::NumberOfProcessors(). Patching here changes the reported value and nothing else.

Platform-specific: sys_info_posix.cc:115, sys_info_win.cc:130, sys_info_fuchsia.cc:110, sys_info_openbsd.cc:33. Also sizes thread pools, so it governs measured parallelism as well as the reported number.
Pure forwarder to ApproximatedDeviceMemory::GetApproximatedDeviceMemory().

Computes and caches the bucketed value from physical_memory_mb_. SetPhysicalMemoryMBForTesting at line 82 is an existing entry point that sets the input and recomputes. The class is a per-process static initialized from two call sites — client_hints.cc:241 in the browser and memory_pressure_listener.cc:63 in the renderer — so it must be correct in both.
Read once during ApproximatedDeviceMemory::Initialize.
Queries the driver live through the command buffer. This is the value JavaScript reads; GPUInfo is a separate path and patching it does not affect this one.

Returns the constant "WebKit WebGL". Line corrected from 4122: that came from codesearch, which indexes main, and was not re-verified at the pinned revision — the exact error the shards were warned about.
Sets gpu_info->gl_renderer and gl_vendor in the GPU process. Independent of the Blink WebGL path — both must be patched and must agree.
Two construction sites at lines 132 and 146; the richer one is gated on WebGPUDeveloperFeaturesEnabled and exposes device, description and driver too.
Reads the browser process's own copy of the ApproximatedDeviceMemory static. Not a source, but proof the profile must reach the browser process.

Top of the browser-process chain. Returns the --user-agent switch value verbatim if present (GetUserAgentFromCommandLine, line 453), otherwise GetUserAgentInternal(). Every other User-Agent emitter in the tree is downstream of this one; there is no second, independent computation of the UA string anywhere. Note the switch path bypasses the whole builder, and user_agent_utils.cc:663 then blanks or freezes UserAgentMetadata when it is used — so --user-agent is not a usable spoof mechanism, it desynchronises the UA string from every client hint.

Assembles product + platform. Line 218: if the --headless switch is present it inserts the literal "Headless" into the product token, which is the single largest UA tell in the tree and is applied before any override we could add downstream of it. Line 228 selects BuildUnifiedPlatformUserAgentFromProduct when kReduceUserAgentMinorVersion is on, which it is by default at this revision (T0 confirms the frozen macOS token).

The OS token in the reduced UA is a compile-time constant per platform, not a reading of the host: macOS is always "Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7" (line 321), Windows always "Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64" (line 323), Linux always "X11; Linux x86_64" (line 327). Consequence: the UA string carries no host OS version at all, so it cannot disagree with a corpus row on OS version — only on OS family. The real OS version has moved entirely into Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version. GetUserAgentPlatform (line 281) and BuildOSCpuInfo/GetOSVersion (lines 435, 382) are the non-reduced path and are dead while kReduceUserAgentMinorVersion is on.
The template itself: "Mozilla/5.0 (%s) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) %s Safari/537.36". The AppleWebKit and Safari version literals are hard-coded here and are the only place they exist.

base::StrCat({"Chrome/", GetMajorVersionNumber(), ".0.0.0"}). This is why the UA string reports 152.0.0.0 while Sec-CH-UA-Full-Version-List reports 152.0.7977.76 — T0 shows exactly that pair. The UA string therefore discloses only the milestone; the build number is disclosed only through client hints. A profile that changes one and not the other breaks coh.ua-version-agreement.

PRODUCT_VERSION from the generated version_info_values.h; GetMajorVersionNumber is base/version_info/version_info.cc:21. Single origin for every version token in this subsystem, and also the seed for brand-list ordering and GREASE (see emit.embedder.greased-brand-version). Compiled in, so the build's own version is what ships unless a profile value is threaded through GetUserAgentMetadata and the UA builder together.

One-line forwarder to embedder_support::GetUserAgent(). Named here because it is the seam every consumer goes through: the renderer bootstrap, the navigation header, and network_context_params->user_agent (line 6963) all read it.
Forwarder to embedder_support::GetUserAgentMetadata().

THE single source of truth for all eleven Client Hint headers and for every navigator.userAgentData value, low and high entropy alike. It is called once in the browser process; the struct it returns is copied to the renderer over mojo at process start (render_process_host_impl.cc:2017) and read again per navigation by the client-hints delegate. Because it is a copy and not a reimplementation, this is materially unlike navigator.deviceMemory: one patch here reaches both processes and both emission sites. Lines 651-655 are the low-entropy set (always populated); 674-683 the high-entropy set, skipped entirely when only_low_entropy_ch is true. Line 663-668 is a trap: a --user-agent switch makes this return blank or low-entropy-only metadata, desynchronising the hints from the UA string.

Compile-time constant per platform: "macOS" (line 633), "Chrome OS"/"Chromium OS" (638-642), otherwise version_info::GetOSType() (line 644, base/version_info/version_info.h:56 — "Windows", "Linux", "Android", ...). Not a runtime OS query, so the JS value and the header value can never disagree with each other in stock Chrome; they can only disagree with navigator.platform, which is a separate constant in Blink.

The only place the real host OS version escapes this subsystem. base::SysInfo::OperatingSystemVersionNumbers formatted "%d.%d.%d" (lines 610-612); empty on Linux and Fuchsia (line 607); on Windows it is the UniversalApiContract version, not the NT version (line 605, GetWindowsPlatformVersion at line 152). T0 measured "26.6.2" against a UA string frozen at 10_15_7 — the two are not expected to agree and a checker that demands they do is wrong.

Real host query. On macOS via base::mac::GetCPUType (line 730); note kTranslatedIntel (Rosetta) reports "arm", so an x86 build on Apple silicon still says arm. On Windows it deliberately corrects the OS lying about WOW: ARM64, WowX86OnARM64 and WowAMD64OnARM64 all return "arm" (lines 722-724). Emits only "arm", "x86" or empty.
Constant "64" on Apple and Fuchsia (line 781); a real query only on Windows and generic POSIX.
base::win::OSInfo::IsWowX86OnAMD64() on Windows, hard false everywhere else (line 939). A non-Windows profile emitting ?1 is self-contradicting and no host can produce it.

Empty string on every non-Android platform (line 867) and on Android desktop; on Android it is base::SysInfo::HardwareModelName() and only on a REL build. T0 measured "" and the header still arrives as sec-ch-ua-model: "" — the hint is sent with an empty value rather than omitted, which is what a desktop reference device looks like.

Hard false on desktop (line 581); on Android/iOS it is purely the presence of the --use-mobile-user-agent switch. Also feeds the form-factors default, so mobile and form-factors cannot be set independently without breaking their own derivation.
Derived, not measured: exactly {"Mobile"} or {"Desktop"} from the mobile bit, plus "XR" on Android XR. T0 measured ["Desktop"] and the header "Desktop".

Builds {GREASE, Chromium, brand} then ShuffleBrandList(list, seed) with seed = the major version number. The brand entry exists only under `#if !BUILDFLAG(CHROMIUM_BRANDING)` (line 166) — a Chromium-branded build emits a TWO-entry list with no "Google Chrome", which no Chrome corpus row can match. This is a build-configuration precondition for this whole subsystem, not something a runtime patch can repair. Order is deterministic, not random: GetRandomOrder (line 237) indexes a fixed permutation table by seed % 6.

The GREASE brand is a pure function of the major version, not randomness: brand = "Not" + chars[seed%11] + "A" + chars[(seed+1)%11] + "Brand" over the 11-character table at line 554, version = {"8","99","24"}[seed%3]. Derived for seed=152: 152%11=9 -> "?", 153%11=10 -> "_", 152%3=2 -> "24", giving "Not?A_Brand";v="24" — which is byte-for-byte what T0 measured. Order likewise: 152%6=2 -> permutation {1,0,2} -> [Chromium, Not?A_Brand, Google Chrome], also exactly T0. So a profile claiming a different major version MUST regenerate both, and copying a captured brand list onto a different claimed version is a contradiction our own generator would create.

RFC 8941 structured-headers serialisation shared by the browser and renderer emission sites, which is why the two produce byte-identical header values from the same struct. SerializeFormFactors at line 65. Not a source — but it is where the exact quoting and ";v=" spelling live, so any hand-built header string must go through it rather than around it.

Pushes GetUserAgent() and GetUserAgentMetadata() into every renderer at process start. This is the proof that the renderer does not recompute either value: it receives a copy. Contrast content/browser/client_hints/client_hints.cc:243 for Device-Memory, where the browser recomputes.

Stores the browser's copy in user_agent_ (line 862) and user_agent_metadata_ (line 864), read back at lines 1162 and 1168. DCHECK(user_agent_.IsNull()) at line 860 means it is written exactly once per renderer process, so a per-profile value must be correct before the first renderer launches.
Forwarder from RenderThreadImpl into Blink's Platform abstraction. UserAgentMetadata at line 359.

Caches Platform::Current()->UserAgent() in user_agent_ (line 949). Both the string (line 936, UserAgentOverride) and the metadata (line 954-963, ApplyUserAgentMetadataOverride) route the CDP/DevTools Emulation.setUserAgentOverride path here. Under axiom A1 this is exactly the mechanism we must NOT use: it is an accessor-level substitution that leaves the browser and network processes on the real value, and it is scoped to the frame, so a worker re-read defeats it.

Pure forwarder: ExecutionContext::UserAgent(), which is LocalDOMWindow::UserAgent (local_dom_window.cc:456 -> FrameLoader::UserAgent) on the main thread and WorkerGlobalScope::UserAgent (worker_global_scope.h:145, a member set at worker creation) in workers. Patching here changes the reported value and nothing else.

`agent.substr(agent.find('/') + 1)` — mechanically everything after the first slash of userAgent(). It cannot diverge from navigator.userAgent by construction, so it needs no separate patch and any patch that made it diverge would be a defect.

THE source. A compile-time constant per build target: "MacIntel", "Win32", "Linux x86_64", "Linux armv81", "iPhone", or "" on Fuchsia. Nothing about the host is read. Reached from both Navigator and WorkerNavigator, so one patch covers window and worker scope.

Virtual override of NavigatorID::platform. On every desktop target it returns GetReducedNavigatorPlatform() unconditionally; only Android with ReduceUserAgentMinorVersion disabled ever falls through to NavigatorID::platform().

The obvious emitter and the WRONG one. It contains the uname(2) call and the "MacIntel"/"Win32" literals, so it reads like the source — but NavigatorBase::platform (navigator_base.cc:54) overrides the virtual for both Navigator and WorkerNavigator, and on every desktop target the uname path is unreachable dead code. Patching this file changes nothing a page can see. Recorded so the next reader does not repeat the mistake.

Window-only override consulting Settings::GetNavigatorPlatformOverride — the CDP Emulation.setUserAgentOverride platform field. WorkerNavigator has no equivalent (worker_navigator.h:37 declares no platform member), so a CDP platform spoof is contradicted by reading navigator.platform inside a Worker. This is the concrete, measurable failure axiom A1 exists to avoid, and it is why the patch belongs at GetReducedNavigatorPlatform instead.

Returns the literal "Google Inc." with a comment warning it must not change. vendorSub at line 54 returns "". Both are Window-only (navigator.idl:26-28); WorkerNavigator does not expose them, which is itself a stable, correct difference.
Returns the literal "20030107". Window-only. T0 confirms.
Three literals: "Mozilla" (47), "Netscape" (51), "Gecko" (86). Exposed on both Navigator and WorkerNavigator via the NavigatorID mixin (navigator.idl:34, worker_navigator.idl:38).

Field-by-field copy of the UserAgentMetadata struct into a fresh NavigatorUAData on every property read. Pure forwarder — every one of the eleven values is already decided in the browser process. The NavigatorUA mixin is included by both Navigator (navigator.idl:38) and WorkerNavigator (worker_navigator.idl:41), and the attribute is [SecureContext] (navigator_ua.idl:8), so userAgentData exists in workers too and one browser-side patch covers both scopes.

Resolves the promise from the already-populated member fields (lines 154-169); no permission check, no gating, no browser round trip. High entropy is a naming convention here, not an access control — any page can read all of it.

Emission site 1 of 2: all eleven Sec-CH-UA-* headers on NAVIGATION requests, in the browser process, from delegate->GetUserAgentMetadata() (line 711). AddUAHeader is line 505; the header-name table is services/network/public/cpp/client_hints.cc:35. Lines 701-707 are the DevTools override hook, and lines 771-783 delete every UA hint when a custom UA is set without metadata — an absence that is itself distinctive.

One line: `return embedder_support::GetUserAgentMetadata();`. Confirms the browser-side header path and the renderer-side JS path terminate at the same function rather than at two independent computations — the opposite of the Device-Memory structure.

Emission site 2 of 2: the same eleven headers on SUBRESOURCE requests, in the renderer, from GetLocalFrameClient()->UserAgentMetadata() (line 675, via line 1309). Structurally the same two-process split that makes Device-Memory dangerous — but here both sites read one browser-computed struct, so a patch at emit.embedder.user-agent-metadata covers both. A renderer-only patch would still fail: navigation headers come from the browser site and would keep the host values. Lines 684-697 in this same function DO recompute Device-Memory locally, so the contrast is visible in one screenful of code.

Sets the User-Agent header on renderer-initiated subresource requests at line 435 (request.SetHTTPUserAgent). Forwards to FrameLoader::UserAgent, i.e. the same cached browser value the JS accessor reads — so navigator.userAgent and the subresource UA header cannot disagree within a frame.

The User-Agent header on navigations, set at lines 409-411 and again at 10541. Returns the per-tab override if set, otherwise GetContentClient()->browser()->GetUserAgent() (line 376). Third writer of this header after the renderer and the network service, all reading one browser value.

The network service's last-resort defaults, applied by URLRequestHttpJob with SetHeaderIfMissing — User-Agent at url_request_http_job.cc:527, Accept-Language at :790 inside AddExtraHeaders (:781). Constructed from NetworkContextParams.user_agent and .accept_language. For User-Agent it is a forwarder of the same browser value; for Accept-Language it is the ONLY writer, which is why that header has a different plumbing path from navigator.languages.

Source of truth for the JavaScript side: GetLanguageListForProfile(profile, prefs kAcceptLanguages), a bare comma list with no q-values. Travels to Blink as RendererPreferences.accept_languages and lands in Page settings at web_view_impl.cc:3805.

Source of truth for the HEADER, and a genuinely separate computation from the JS path. Same underlying pref, but run through ReduceAcceptLanguageUtils::GetLanguagesWithMaxCount, then net::HttpUtil::ExpandLanguageList and GenerateAcceptLanguageHeader (ComputeAcceptLanguageFromPref, line 211), which append q-values and expand base languages. Written into NetworkContextParams at line 1356. T0 shows the divergent shapes side by side: navigator.languages ["en-US","en"] against Accept-Language "en-US,en;q=0.9". Two processes, two transforms, one pref — set one and not the other and the header contradicts JavaScript exactly as Device-Memory does.
Copies RendererPreferences.accept_languages into Page settings and dispatches languagechange when it differs (lines 3801-3806).

Window path reads Page settings; the worker path is worker_navigator.cc:43, reading WorkerOrWorkletGlobalScope::GetAcceptLanguages, which is fed from the same RendererPreferences. Two accessors, one upstream value — so worker and window agree in stock Chrome and must continue to.

Splits and sanitises the accept-languages string (ParseAndSanitize, line 17), then — lines 94-99 — truncates the list to its first entry when network::features::kReduceAcceptLanguage is enabled. T0 returned two entries, so that feature is off at this revision and the list is the full pref. navigator.language is just languages().front() (line 39). Lines 55-59 and 72-79 are the CDP Network.setUserAgentOverride acceptLanguage probe, an accessor-level override forbidden by axiom A1.

Fallback only: used when the accept-languages string is empty (navigator_language.cc:31). Reads Platform::Current()->DefaultLocale(), i.e. the host UI locale, so an empty pref leaks the real machine locale. DefaultLanguage at line 94.

Scans PluginData for an "application/pdf" mime type; PluginData is populated from the browser process. When true the constructor (line 55) synthesises the five spec-mandated fake plugin names with filename "internal-pdf-viewer" — so navigator.plugins and navigator.pdfViewerEnabled are one bit, not two independent observables, and cannot be made to disagree.

One-line forwarder to plugins(window)->IsPdfViewerAvailable(). Window-only: navigator_plugins.idl:12 has no Worker exposure, so pdfViewerEnabled is undefined in a worker and that asymmetry is correct stock behaviour.

The source: registers the internal PDF plugin with mime type application/pdf, entirely inside `#if BUILDFLAG(ENABLE_PDF)` (lines 124-145). The observable is therefore decided by a GN arg, not by anything runtime. A build with enable_pdf=false reports pdfViewerEnabled false and an empty navigator.plugins while still claiming to be Chrome — a build-configuration failure no patch can reach.
The #if !BUILDFLAG(CHROMIUM_BRANDING) guard is the whole mechanism; supplying brand unconditionally reaches every brand-list consumer.
product.insert(0, "Headless") behind a --headless switch check, upstream of the UA string and every header derived from it.

The macOS origin of every display value in this shard. bounds <- NSScreen.frame (line 85/90), work_area <- NSScreen.visibleFrame with a y-flip for the primary screen (lines 92-103) — this is the emitter that produces the measured 33px menu-bar top inset and the 83px dock bottom inset. device_scale_factor <- NSScreen.backingScaleFactor (line 105-110). color_depth is NOT the real framebuffer depth: lines 172-181 set it to exactly 30/10 when maximumPotentialExtendedDynamicRangeColorComponentValue > 1 and 24/8 otherwise, so it is a one-bit HDR flag wearing a bit-depth's clothes. Per-platform siblings: ui/display/win/screen_win.cc, ui/display/screen_ozone.cc, ui/display/android/. Patching here fixes every downstream consumer in every process at once.

Second, independent write path for color_depth/depth_per_component: any call that installs a DisplayColorSpacesRef re-derives them from color_spaces->SupportsHDR(), 30/10 when true and 24/8 when false (lines 346-352). So screen.colorDepth, the CSS `color` feature and `dynamic-range` are not three facts but one, and a patch that sets color_depth without setting the color spaces will be silently overwritten the next time the display's color profile is (re)applied.

The single choke point where a display::Display becomes the display::ScreenInfo that is shipped to renderers. rect <- bounds (:18), available_rect <- work_area (:20), device_scale_factor (:21), depth <- color_depth (:24), depth_per_component (:25), is_monochrome (:26), orientation_angle <- PanelRotationAsDegree (:30), orientation_type <- GetOrientationTypeForDesktop (:48). is_extended is computed here and nowhere else, as `screen && screen->GetNumDisplays() > 1` (:55) — it is a live count of the browser's displays, not a field carried on the Display. One patch here covers every renderer and every frame.

Waypoint. Loops GetAllDisplays() and calls DisplayToScreenInfo for each (:223), picking current and primary ids. Interesting only because it builds the whole multi-display list that screen.isExtended and getScreenDetails() expose: a profile claiming one display must shorten this list, not merely flip a boolean.
Waypoint. Picks the display nearest the widget's NativeView (or the primary display) and caches the result in RenderWidgetHostViewBase::screen_infos_, which GetScreenInfos() at :694 hands back.

THE PROCESS BOUNDARY. `visual_properties.screen_infos = GetScreenInfos()` at :1058, sent over blink.mojom.PlatformWidget::UpdateVisualProperties (third_party/blink/public/mojom/widget/platform_widget.mojom:106) as display.mojom.ScreenInfos (visual_properties.mojom:18). Everything a page can read about the physical display arrives in the renderer through this one message. Note :1063-1069: when hardware acceleration is off the browser rewrites HDR and high bit depth out of every ScreenInfo here, so colorDepth silently drops 30 -> 24 — a software-rendering configuration contradicts an HDR profile with no patch involved.

Browser origin of window.outerWidth/outerHeight/screenX/screenY. Reads view_->GetViewBoundsWithoutTransform() and view_->GetBoundsInScreenWithoutTransform() (:665-671) — the real OS window geometry — and pushes them over blink.mojom.PlatformWidget::UpdateScreenRects (platform_widget.mojom:111). A second mojo channel, separate from VisualProperties; a patch that only touches ScreenInfos leaves the window rect real.

THE deviceMemory PATTERN, REPEATED. On navigation requests the browser computes the DPR header itself: GetDeviceScaleFactor() at :142 reads display::Screen::Get()->GetPrimaryDisplay().device_scale_factor() directly from the browser's own display list, multiplied by GetZoomFactor() at :153 which reads HostZoomMap. It never consults the renderer. A renderer-only patch to LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio therefore makes Sec-CH-DPR on the navigation contradict window.devicePixelRatio in the document it loads. Two further stock divergences worth knowing: it uses the PRIMARY display, not the display the window is on, and it uses the host zoom map's level rather than the frame's composed layout zoom.

Browser-side origin of Sec-CH-Viewport-Width/Height on navigation requests: view->GetVisibleViewportSize() at :297, then divided by the HostZoomMap zoom factor in GetScaledViewportSize (:334-338). Independent of the renderer's own LocalFrameView size.

The renderer's entire copy of display state. screen_infos_ is assigned from the browser's VisualProperties at :248 (widget construction) and :1884 (every later update), and UpdateVisualProperties at :479 is where the mojo payload lands. This is the single renderer-side chokepoint and the correct renderer patch point — but it is a waypoint, not a source: the browser process still holds the host's real display and still uses it for Sec-CH-DPR (emit.browser.client-hints-dpr), chrome://settings, and window placement.

Existing renderer-side override of exactly these fields, driven by CDP Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride. It copies original_screen_infos_, rewrites rect (:109-112), device_scale_factor (:121-122) and orientation (:127-130), then calls SetScreenInfoAndSize. Recorded as a shape reference and as a warning: it keeps original_screen_infos_ intact, is renderer-local, and leaves the browser holding the truth — which is precisely the failure mode a profile patch must avoid. Under A1 we do not drive it; we replace the value upstream.

Pure forwarder: `return frame.GetWidgetForLocalRoot()->GetScreenInfos();`. Every Blink consumer of display state — Screen, MediaValues, ScreenOrientationController, LocalDOMWindow — funnels through this one method or its GetScreenInfo() sibling.

Selects the ScreenInfo matching display_id_ out of the ScreenInfos list; falls back to a static all-zero ScreenInfo when the id is not found (:195-196), which is why a screen object outliving its display reports zeros rather than stale values.

The one function behind width(), height(), availWidth(), availHeight(), availLeft() and availTop() (screen.cc:90-143): `available ? screen_info.available_rect : screen_info.rect`. Two quirk paths scale the result — ReportScreenSizeInPhysicalPixelsQuirk multiplies by device_scale_factor (:178) and a text-scale meta tag multiplies by text_scale_multiplier (:180) — both off on desktop. Note availLeft/availTop are the rect's ORIGIN in virtual-screen coordinates, so on a secondary monitor they are non-zero (and can be negative) even with no menu bar involved.

Forwards ScreenInfo::depth, substituting the spec's 24 when depth is 0 (:112-114). Screen::pixelDepth() at :117 is literally `return colorDepth();` — the two can never disagree, so a detector comparing them learns nothing and a patch must not treat them as two values.

Returns false unless the window-management permissions policy is enabled (:164-167), then forwards ScreenInfo::is_extended. Readable without a permission PROMPT — the policy gate is not the permission gate — so it is a free multi-monitor probe on any first-party page.

symbol: blink::ScreenDetailed::left / top / isPrimary / isInternal / devicePixelRatio / label / hdrHeadroom
notes: Forwards ScreenInfo fields that no other API exposes: label() at :134 returns the OS display name string, isInternal() at :122 distinguishes a laptop panel from an external monitor, hdrHeadroom() at :140 and the eight colour-primary getters from :150 expose the display's measured ICC primaries and white point as floats. Also a zoom oracle: devicePixelRatio() at :128 returns the RAW ScreenInfo::device_scale_factor, while window.devicePixelRatio returns DSF x page zoom, so comparing the two reveals the page zoom level exactly.

Copies ScreenInfo::orientation_type and orientation_angle into the ScreenOrientation object (:115-129); ScreenOrientation::type()/angle() at screen_orientation.cc:90/94 just read the copy. When the type is undefined it recomputes from screen_info.rect's aspect (:122-123). LocalDOMWindow::orientation() (local_dom_window.cc:1196) is a separate legacy reader of the same orientation_angle, remapping 270 to -90.

DEVICE PIXEL RATIO IS NOT A PASSTHROUGH. `ratio = page_->InspectorDeviceScaleFactorOverride(); ratio *= LayoutZoomFactor();`. LayoutZoomFactor is composed in WebFrameWidgetImpl::SetZoomInternal (web_frame_widget_impl.cc:2515-2518) as device_scale_factor * ZoomLevelToZoomFactor(zoom_level) * css_zoom_factor, where device_scale_factor is WebViewImpl::ZoomFactorForViewportLayout() (web_view_impl.h:182), itself set from ScreenInfo::device_scale_factor in WebFrameWidgetImpl::DidUpdateSurfaceAndScreen (:5419). So page zoom IS folded in: at 110% zoom on a 2x display window.devicePixelRatio is 2.2, not 2. A patch that pins this function to a constant destroys the zoom relationship and makes every zoom level report the same ratio, which no real browser does. Patch ScreenInfo::device_scale_factor upstream instead and let the multiplication stand. This is the only place the product is formed, and window.devicePixelRatio, the CSS `resolution` / `-webkit-device-pixel-ratio` features and the renderer's own DPR client hint all read it.

Pure forwarder to LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio(). Patching here would leave the CSS `resolution` media feature and the DPR client hint reporting the host's real ratio — an in-page contradiction detectable with one matchMedia call.
`return frame->DevicePixelRatio();` — identical source to window.devicePixelRatio.

Backs both `resolution` (:605) and `-webkit-device-pixel-ratio` (:595) plus their min-/max- forms. For media type screen, actual_resolution = ClampTo<float>(media_values.DevicePixelRatio()) (:557); for print it is hardcoded 300/96 dppx (:562). dpcm comparisons are rounded to 2 decimal places (:585-588), which is the only place the value is quantised.

Both read ChromeClient::GetScreenInfo(*frame).rect (:169, :181) — the same rect as screen.width/height, so `device-width` and screen.width cannot be made to disagree by patching ScreenInfo, and MUST not be patched separately. CalculateDeviceHeight is at :177.

`color` returns ScreenInfo::depth_per_component, or 0 when is_monochrome (:212-215). `monochrome` (:219) is the mirror image: depth_per_component when is_monochrome, else 0. So the two features are one bit plus one number, and (color: 10) is exactly (colorDepth: 30) restated. `color-index` is not backed by MediaValues at all — ColorIndexMediaFeatureEval (media_query_evaluator.cc:347) compares against the literal 0 with a comment saying Chromium assumes no indexed displays exist. It is a constant and must stay one.
Returns the Page's MediaFeatureOverrides value if one is set — the CDP Emulation.setEmulatedMedia path — otherwise color_space_utilities::GetColorSpaceGamut(GetScreenInfo(*frame)).

Derives the gamut bucket from ScreenInfo::display_color_spaces.GetScreenInfoColorSpace(). Two paths: any HDR colour space short-circuits to P3 (:26-27), otherwise the profile is run through skcms and scored, with hard thresholds mapping the score to sRGB / P3 / Rec2020 (:62-79). The value therefore follows from the display colour space the browser installed; it is derived, not stored, so it is set by choosing a colour space, not by writing a bucket.

`GetScreenInfo(*frame).display_color_spaces.SupportsHDR()`. DynamicRangeMediaFeatureEval (media_query_evaluator.cc:513) returns true unconditionally for `standard` and this value for `high`; `video-dynamic-range` at :535 is documented as an alias and returns the same answer. Same input as the 30-bit colour depth, so HDR is one fact with three faces.

The CSS `orientation` feature is VIEWPORT orientation, not display orientation: it compares media_values.Width() against Height() (:472-479) and treats a square viewport as portrait. It has no connection to screen.orientation.type, and a tall narrow window on a landscape monitor legitimately reports portrait in CSS and landscape-primary on screen.orientation. Any coherence rule forcing them equal would be wrong.

Returns window_screen_rect_, set only from the browser's UpdateScreenRects (:576-577, :1946-1947), or a pending rect after a script-driven move/resize. ChromeClientImpl::RootWindowRect (chrome_client_impl.cc:305) is the Blink-facing wrapper.

outerHeight :1669, outerWidth :1701. Both return ChromeClient::RootWindowRect(*frame) dimensions unscaled on desktop. Two behaviours worth recording: inside a fenced frame tree they return innerWidth/innerHeight instead (:1678-1680, :1710-1712), and unlike innerWidth they are NOT divided by the zoom factor — so outerWidth/innerWidth is a zoom oracle independent of devicePixelRatio.

screenX :1784, screenY :1809; window.screenLeft/screenTop (window.idl:198-199) are aliases. Both return RootWindowRect origin in virtual-screen coordinates, so on a multi-monitor host they leak the window's position across the whole desktop — including negative coordinates for a monitor left of or above the primary, which contradicts a single-display profile immediately.

innerHeight :1766, innerWidth :1775. Both are AdjustForAbsoluteZoom::AdjustInt(GetViewportSize(), LocalFrame::LayoutZoomFactor()) — the LayoutFrameView size in CSS pixels. The view size originates in the browser as VisualProperties::new_size; the CSS-pixel conversion happens here. Because the divisor is LayoutZoomFactor (DSF x zoom x css zoom), inner size and devicePixelRatio move together and a patch to one without the other breaks their product.

width :139, height :161, scale :183, offsetLeft :63, offsetTop :74. For the outermost main frame these forward to Page::GetVisualViewport(); for subframes they compute from the layout viewport's VisibleContentRect excluding scrollbars, divided by LayoutZoomFactor. Nothing here reads ScreenInfo.

Width :494 and Height :501 return VisibleWidthCSSPx()/VisibleHeightCSSPx() (:524, :533), built from VisibleRect (:439) which takes size_ (set by SetSize at :395 from the widget size), optionally excludes scrollbars, adds browser_controls_adjustment_ and divides by the pinch scale (:444-450). Pure window and pinch-zoom state; carries no display identity.

getClientRects :3351, GetClientRectsNoAdjustment :3365, GetBoundingClientRectNoLifecycleUpdateNoAdjustment :3384, GetBoundingClientRect :3411, GetBoundingClientRectForBinding :3417. All of them do the same three things: force layout, call Element::ClientQuads (:3315) which calls LayoutObject::AbsoluteQuads, take bounding boxes, and hand the result to Document::AdjustRectForScrollAndAbsoluteZoom. No arithmetic of its own — the numbers are already fixed by the time this function sees them, which is exactly why a patch here would be a fabrication rather than a value.

Where rect numbers actually come from: the laid-out geometry, mapped to absolute coordinates. QuadsInAncestor is at :2474 and dispatches to the virtual QuadsInAncestorInternal (:3622), overridden per layout-object class. The storage is LayoutUnit, a fixed-point type holding multiples of 1/64 px (third_party/blink/renderer/platform/geometry/layout_unit.h:67, kFixedPointDenominator = 1 << kFractionalBits at :91). That constant is the whole explanation of the competitor artifact recorded in coh.layout-integer-positions: -10000.015625 is -10000 - 1/64 and -0.03125 is -2/64, i.e. a +-1 and +-2 perturbation of the raw LayoutUnit storage. Noise injected anywhere in this path is quantised to 1/64 px and is therefore identifiable as tampering rather than as a different device. The correct treatment is to leave this path untouched and make its inputs — fonts, zoom, DSF — correct.

Divides the absolute rect by LocalFrame::LayoutZoomFactor() when StandardizedBrowserZoom is enabled, else by ComputedStyle::EffectiveZoom (:112-120); the quad form is at :100 and the int form used by innerWidth/innerHeight at :44. The last transform applied to a client rect and the obvious place to inject noise — which is why it is named here explicitly as a place NOT to patch.

getComputedStyle's engine (window.getComputedStyle at local_dom_window.cc:1928). Forces style and layout, then dispatches to the per-property CSSProperty::CSSValueFromComputedStyle (:387) with CSSValuePhase::kResolvedValue. For layout-dependent properties — width, height, inline-size, top/left on a positioned box — the resolved value is read back off the same LayoutObject that produced the client rects, which is what makes rect-vs-computed-style comparison a valid consistency check rather than two independent reads.

The renderer's own client-hint emitter, used for SUBRESOURCE requests. GetDevicePixelRatio (:1380) returns Document::DevicePixelRatio() = LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio(), written into DPR at :886 and into Sec-CH-Width/Resource-Width at :914-931. Viewport-Width/Height come from LocalFrameView::ViewportWidth()/ViewportHeight() (local_frame_view.cc:4527/4532) at :901-911, which are the layout size divided by absolute zoom — the same quantity as window.innerWidth. So the same header has two producers split by request type: browser for the navigation, renderer for every subresource. Arbiter: renamed from emit.blink.frame-fetch-context-client-hints. Shard 1 mapped AddClientHintsIfNecessary at line 641 for the Sec-CH-UA family and shard 2 mapped GetDevicePixelRatio at line 1380 for DPR and viewport; these are different functions in one file that independently received the same id.

The origin of GL_RENDERER as JavaScript sees it. Builds "ANGLE (<vendor>, <renderer>, <version>)" from the backend Display at :3592-3598. Lines :3570-3577 read the ANGLE_GL_RENDERER environment variable (Android property debug.angle.gl_renderer) and, when non-empty, return it verbatim in place of the whole constructed string; initVendorString at :3578 does the same for ANGLE_GL_VENDOR. The command buffer does NOT synthesise GL_RENDERER or GL_VENDOR - they fall through the default branch of GLES2DecoderPassthroughImpl::DoGetString to glGetStringFn - so both the Blink WebGL path and gpu_info_collector's GetGLString(GL_RENDERER) terminate here. This makes the existing emit.blink.webgl-unmasked-renderer a waypoint over the command buffer rather than the origin; arbiter should decide whether to downgrade its is_source_of_truth. An existing env-var hook means the string can be changed without touching Blink at all.

Returns "ANGLE Metal Renderer" + ": " + MTLDevice.name. The Metal device name is the only genuinely GPU-model-derived value in the entire WebGL surface; every other limit on this backend is a constant (see emit.angle.display-mtl-caps).

The WebGL limit set on the Metal backend is hard-coded here, not queried from the GPU: maxElementIndex 2^32-2 (:725), max3DTextureSize 2048 (:726), max2DTextureSize 16384 (:728), maxVaryingVectors 31-1 (:730), maxVertexOutputComponents = maxFragmentInputComponents = 124-4 (:731), maxAliasedPointSize 511 (:760), min/maxAliasedLineWidth 1.0 (:761-762), maxSamples from the format table (:802), all float precisions setIEEEFloat (:818-823), all int precisions setTwosComplementInt(32) (:825-830), minProgramTexelOffset -8 / maxProgramTexelOffset 7 later in the same function. Every one of these matches the T0 capture exactly. Consequence: the WebGL parameter and precision dump identifies the ANGLE backend and the OS, not the GPU model - an M1 and an M4 Max return the same numbers. Each other backend has its own equivalent (RendererVk, Renderer11, RendererGL), which is why the dump changes wholesale when the backend changes.

GL_VERSION and GL_SHADING_LANGUAGE_VERSION are synthesised in the GPU process and never reach the driver (:1795-1799); GL_EXTENSIONS is rebuilt from FeatureInfo (:1801-1805); everything else, GL_RENDERER and GL_VENDOR included, falls through to api()->glGetStringFn at :1807.

Returns the literal "OpenGL ES 3.0 Chromium" or "OpenGL ES 2.0 Chromium" depending only on whether the context is ES3. GetServiceShadingLanguageVersionString at :399 does the same for "OpenGL ES GLSL ES 3.0 Chromium" / "OpenGL ES GLSL ES 1.0 Chromium". No device input at all.

GL_VERSION at :4187 wraps the command-buffer string as "WebGL 1.0 (<inner>)"; GL_SHADING_LANGUAGE_VERSION at :4125 wraps it as "WebGL GLSL ES 1.0 (<inner>)"; GL_VENDOR at :4185 returns the constant "WebKit". The WebGL2 overrides are at webgl2_rendering_context_base.cc:4844 and :4851 with "WebGL 2.0 (" and "WebGL GLSL ES 3.00 (". Every component is a constant; nothing here varies by device.

The WebGL1 dispatcher. Almost every case forwards to a Get*Parameter helper; the exceptions worth knowing are GL_RENDERER (:4107, constant "WebKit WebGL" - note docs/SUBSYSTEMS.md and emit.blink.webgl-masked-renderer record 4122, which is wrong at this revision), GL_VENDOR (:4185), GL_ALPHA_BITS (:4002, forced to 0 when the drawing buffer must preserve alpha), GL_DEPTH_BITS (:4039) and GL_STENCIL_BITS (:4062), both forced to 0 when the creation attribute was not asked for, and GL_COMPRESSED_TEXTURE_FORMATS (:4032), which returns a Blink-maintained list.

Forwards ContextGL()->GetIntegerv verbatim with no clamping (the only special case is returning null for IMPLEMENTATION_COLOR_READ_* when the framebuffer is incomplete). Sibling helpers: GetBooleanParameter :7878, GetFloatParameter :7904, GetUnsignedIntParameter :7945, GetWebGLFloatArrayParameter :7954, GetWebGLIntArrayParameter :7978. Patching any of these is patching an accessor, not an emitter - the values originate in the ANGLE caps table.

Handles the WebGL2-only pnames then falls through to the WebGL1 switch at :5053. MAX_CLIENT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_WEBGL (:4869) returns the Blink constant kMaxClientWaitTimeout = 0u (:114), and MAX_SERVER_WAIT_TIMEOUT likewise reads 0 in the capture - neither is a device value. Several limits go through GetInt64Parameter, which is why MAX_ELEMENT_INDEX reads 4294967294.

Iterates extensions_ in registration order and pushes those passing ExtensionSupportedAndAllowed. The result is never sorted, so the returned order IS the registration order - a list returned in any other order is wrong by construction.

39 RegisterExtension<> calls at :104-144. The T0 capture returns exactly 39 extensions in exactly this order, so on this device every registered WebGL1 extension is supported and the order is fully determined here.

40 RegisterExtension<> calls at :83-124. The T0 capture returns 36. The four absent are OVRMultiview2 (not supported on the Metal backend) and the three registered with kDraftExtension - WebGLDrawInstancedBaseVertexBaseInstance (:115), WebGLMultiDrawInstancedBaseVertexBaseInstance (:118) and WebGLShaderPixelLocalStorage (:123) - which is exactly what the gate in emit.blink.webgl-extension-supported-and-allowed predicts.

Four gates: draft extensions need WebGLDraftExtensionsEnabled, developer extensions need WebGLDeveloperExtensionsEnabled, tracker->Supported(this) asks the backend, and disabled_extensions_ removes anything the GPU config disabled. The third gate is where the ANGLE backend enters the extension list, and the fourth is where the GPU blocklist does.

Splits GpuFeatureInfo::disabled_webgl_extensions on spaces into disabled_extensions_ at :1381-1389. This is the concrete, page-observable consequence of a GPU blocklist decision: the blocklist is keyed on GPUInfo, and the extension list a page reads is filtered by it. It is the reason gpuinfo.gl-renderer is in scope even though the string itself is not page-readable.

Collects disabled_webgl_extensions from every matched entry. In gpu_driver_bug_list.json at this revision only one entry (id 257, a test entry) uses this field, but the sibling GetDisabledExtensions at :773 - which collects plain GL extensions and is used by 22 real entries - feeds GpuFeatureInfo::disabled_extensions and thence GpuFeatureInfo::ApplyToGLContext -> SetDisabledGLExtensions, which removes GL extensions and so removes the WebGL extensions that depend on them.
gl_context->SetDisabledGLExtensions(disabled_extensions) at :33. The hop from a blocklist decision to a GL extension string the page can enumerate.

The single place where GPUInfo becomes configuration. Runs the blocklist (gpu/config/software_rendering_list.json, 84 entries) at :647-666 and the driver bug list (gpu/config/gpu_driver_bug_list.json, 253 entries) at :739-769, then merges command-line overrides at :771. Both lists key exclusively on GPUInfo fields - vendor_id appears in 116 entries, gl_vendor 74, driver_version 59, gl_renderer 58, device_id 33, plus os, driver_vendor, gl_extensions, gl_version, machine_model_name and the intel_gpu_series/generation shorthands. Therefore: if GPUInfo is made to describe the profile's device before this call, the entire downstream configuration - feature status, disabled extensions, workaround set, and the MSAA count that changes rendered pixels - follows the claimed device automatically, using Chromium's own tables. That is the cheapest available lever on the render, and it needs no per-pixel interference.

Every one of the 142 workaround names in gpu/config/gpu_workaround_list.txt is also a command-line switch of the same name (kFeatureList is built from the same GPU_OP macro list at :22-28, and build_workaround_header.py:46 shows the name is the txt line verbatim). Switch present forces the workaround on; switch value "0" forces it off. Workarounds observable from a page include webgl_or_caps_max_texture_size_limit_4096 and _8192 (change MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE), max_msaa_sample_count_2 and _4 (change SAMPLES and the rendered edge pixels), msaa_is_slow, msaa_is_slow_2, disable_chromium_framebuffer_multisample, disable_webgl_rgb_multisampling_usage and use_eqaa_storage_samples_2. The switch lives on the GPU process command line and is not readable from a renderer, so using it adds no observable of its own.

Validates the enums then forwards ContextGL()->GetShaderPrecisionFormat at :4512 and wraps the result. No clamping, no substitution: the twelve triples a page can read come straight from the ANGLE backend's caps.

Echoes the author's creation attributes, then corrects four of them against reality: depth and stencil are cleared if the drawing buffer lacks those buffers (:3793-3796), antialias is replaced by GetDrawingBuffer()->Multisample() (:3797), xrCompatible and desynchronized come from context state. Only antialias carries device information, and it is decided in DrawingBuffer::Initialize.

Where the MSAA configuration that produces the rendered bytes is fixed. max_sample_count is read from GL_MAX_SAMPLES_ANGLE (:944); implicit resolve is force-disabled on macOS and iOS (:965-969) and whenever Skia Graphite is enabled (:958-962); the mode is chosen at :970-989; sample_count_ = min(webgl_preferences.msaa_sample_count, max_sample_count) at :991-992; eqaa_storage_sample_count_ is forced to 2 by the USE_EQAA_STORAGE_SAMPLES_2 workaround (:993-996). sample_count_ is then used for the renderbuffer allocation at :1477, :1482 and :1841-1845, so it is not a reported number, it is the render.

Source of truth for msaa_sample_count. Struct defaults are anti_aliasing_mode kAntialiasingModeUnspecified, msaa_sample_count 4, eqaa_storage_sample_count 4 (third_party/blink/public/platform/web_graphics_context_3d_provider.h:76-83). The MAX_MSAA_SAMPLE_COUNT_2 workaround forces 2 at :96-97; --webgl-msaa-sample-count overrides the count at :99-105; --webgl-antialiasing-mode selects none/explicit/implicit at :107-119; --max-active-webgl-contexts overrides the context caps at :129-139. Computed once into a function-local static, so it is fixed for the life of the renderer process - which is what makes it a profile setting rather than per-call behaviour.

Validates the destination view and format, calls ClearIfComposited, then reads the drawing buffer through the command buffer into the caller's ArrayBufferView. The WebGL2 entry points at webgl2_rendering_context_base.cc:833, :853 and :874 funnel into the same helper. There is no value stored here to overwrite - the bytes are whatever the GPU actually rendered, which is why this surface is escalated rather than assigned a spoof verdict.

Takes a StaticBitmapImage snapshot (:469) and readPixels into the ImageData buffer (:505-511). Two behaviours matter for determinism: when willReadFrequently is undefined, read_count_ is incremented and acceleration is disabled once it reaches kFallbackToCPUAfterReadbacks = 2 (base_rendering_context_2d.h:78, check at :461-466), so the first readback of a canvas can come from GPU raster and later ones from CPU raster; and a console warning is emitted on the second readback (:441-455), which is itself a weak observable.

Snapshot -> ImageDataBuffer -> ImageDataBuffer::ToDataURL. Returns the literal "data:," when the canvas is not paintable (:1282). The public entry at :1327 throws on a tainted canvas before reaching here. toBlob at :1351 takes the same encoding path.

Given identical pixels the encoded byte stream is a pure function of build constants: PNG through SkPngRustEncoder at CompressionLevel::kLow (:61), JPEG at default quality 92 (ComputeJpegQuality :109-114) with AlphaOption::kBlendOnBlack and Downsample::k444 only at quality 100 (:49-55), WebP at default quality 80 and lossless-at-75 when quality is exactly 1.0 (ComputeWebpOptions :116-131). No device input, no host input. Note the PNG encoder is the Rust one at this revision, so PNG bytes are Chromium-version-specific.

Decides whether canvas 2D is rastered on the GPU or the CPU, which is the largest single input to the rendered bytes after the backend itself. Gates: non-2D contexts never accelerate (:1476); RuntimeEnabledFeatures::Accelerated2dCanvasEnabled (:1480), set from --disable-accelerated-2d-canvas via web_contents_impl.cc:3816-3817; and the small-canvas cutoff kMinimumAccelerated2dCanvasSize = 128*129 (:168) at :1485-1496, which is guarded by AcceleratedSmallCanvasesEnabled. That feature is status "stable" (runtime_enabled_features.json5:229-230) and is only ever cleared on Android, so on desktop the cutoff does not apply and a typical small fingerprinting canvas IS GPU-rastered. SetPreferred2DRasterMode is chosen at :1562-1564 and downgraded to kPreferCPU when willReadFrequently is true.

Independent of HTMLCanvasElement::ShouldAccelerate: it asks Accelerated2DCanvasFeatureEnabled against SharedGpuContext::ContextProviderWrapper() and has no small-canvas cutoff and no willReadFrequently input. So an OffscreenCanvas in a worker and an HTMLCanvasElement on the main thread can be rastered by different backends for the same drawing operations.
The OffscreenCanvas readback path, alongside transferToImageBitmap at :296. Uses the same ImageEncoder constants as toDataURL.

ToCanvasRenderingContext2DSettings(CreationAttributes()) - a verbatim echo of what the author asked for, plus IDL defaults. Unlike the WebGL equivalent nothing is corrected against reality, so no device information reaches the page here.

width from MeasureRuns, i.e. shaping (:110-111); actualBoundingBoxLeft/Right from glyph bounds (:127-128); fontBoundingBoxAscent/Descent from FontMetrics with the baseline table applied (:132-139); em heights from NormalizedTypoAscentAndDescent (:144-146); hanging and ideographic baselines from the font's baseline table with an ascent-percentage fallback (:149-168). Every single input is font data. There is no GPU, rasteriser or compositor input, so this surface belongs to the fonts-text subsystem rather than gpu-graphics.

Rejects non-finite coordinates and non-invertible transforms, inverse-maps the point through the CTM, then calls Path::Contains, i.e. SkPath::contains. Pure CPU floating-point path arithmetic - no rasterisation, no font, no GPU. isPointInStroke at :1881 is the stroke-geometry sibling and takes stroke width and join style into account but is likewise device-independent.

Where canvas text rasterisation is configured on macOS: SkFont::Edging is kSubpixelAntiAlias, kAntiAlias or kAlias depending on should_antialias and should_smooth_fonts (:244-250); embedded bitmaps are always off (:252); embolden and skew implement synthetic bold/italic (:255-256); setSubpixel and setLinearMetrics follow should_subpixel_position (:257-261); hinting is forced to kNone for -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased and text-rendering:geometricPrecision (:265-270). These flags plus the font file itself determine the glyph coverage bytes a canvas text fingerprint reads. Platform-specific: the Linux/Windows equivalents take their values from RendererPreferences instead.

symbol: blink::RendererPreferences (should_antialias_text, text_contrast, text_gamma, hinting, use_autohinter, use_bitmaps, subpixel_rendering, use_subpixel_positioning)
notes: Eight fields at :36-44 that decide text rasterisation on the platforms that do not get it from the OS text engine. On Linux they are derived from the host's fontconfig and desktop settings, which makes them a host leak into canvas text, and they are pushed to the renderer as preferences - so they are settable from a profile without patching any rasteriser. text_contrast and text_gamma default to SK_GAMMA_CONTRAST/SK_GAMMA_EXPONENT build constants.

Maps --use-angle to an ANGLE DisplayType. The switch values are enumerated in ui/gl/gl_switches.cc:35-56 (default, d3d11, d3d11on12, d3d11-warp, d3d11-warp-webgl, gl, gl-egl, gles, gles-egl, null, vulkan, swiftshader, swiftshader-webgl, metal, plus the *-null test variants) and the switch itself is kUseANGLE at :93. Critically, each branch is guarded by a supports_angle_* flag: Metal is only offered where the Apple backend is compiled in (:77-80, :152-160), D3D11 only on Windows (:88-102), so the backend is runtime-selectable but bounded by the host OS. kDefaultANGLEMetal (:45-46) decides the macOS default. gl_implementation.cc:349-360 infers --use-gl=angle when only --use-angle is given.

Calls wgpu::Adapter::GetFeatures and maps each wgpu::FeatureName that has a V8 enum onto the GPUSupportedFeatures set; features Blink has no enum for are silently dropped (:43-48). Invoked from the GPUAdapter constructor at :116, i.e. once per adapter. The real source is Dawn's adapter, one layer below Blink, in the same relationship as ANGLE has to WebGL.

Returns RGBA8Unorm on Android and Linux and BGRA8Unorm on every other platform - a compile-time constant with no device, driver or backend input. The V8 entry point is getPreferredCanvasFormat at :415. This makes it a direct OS assertion: a Linux host answers "rgba8unorm" and contradicts any macOS or Windows claim in one property read.

Sets accelerated_2d_canvas_enabled from --disable-accelerated-2d-canvas (:3816-3817), antialiased_2d_canvas_disabled from --disable-2d-canvas-antialiasing (:3821-3822) and antialiased_clips_2d_canvas_enabled from --disable-2d-canvas-clip-antialiasing (:3823-3824). These reach Blink through WebViewImpl::SetPreferences at third_party/blink/renderer/core/exported/web_view_impl.cc:1670-1682 and are consumed for clip antialiasing at canvas_rendering_context_2d.cc:211. Three existing, deterministic, per-profile controls over canvas 2D rendered bytes that require no per-pixel interference.
